outcome: No new result on the conjecture itself appeared after 26 January 2024 that I could find: it remains open in general, with partial results on Dutch windmills, triangular snakes and two named families, all first written before the window. The in-window items are journal appearances of 2020 and 2021 preprints (AJC 91(2), issue dated Feb 2025; Ars Combinatoria 159(1), 2024 per DBLP), plus discounted papers on quadrangular cacti (2025), on a game on graphs that misstates the conjecture (2020), on the tree parent (Nov 2025) and an LLM evaluation on a different graph question (Feb 2026).
problem_asks: The bullet, read from its statement alone: (1) the quantifier runs over every triangular cactus, a connected graph in which every block is a triangle, of any size and shape; (2) each such cactus admits a graceful labelling or a nearly graceful labelling. Terms as the sources use them: graceful = an injective vertex labelling into {0,...,m} for a graph with m edges whose edge labels |f(u)-f(v)| are exactly {1,...,m}; nearly graceful = a close variant whose edge labels are {1,...,m-1,m+1}, with sources disagreeing on whether the vertex labels range over {0,...,m} or {0,...,m+1}. The bullet itself does not say which type a given cactus should get. The 1988 source and the later literature attach a sharper reading: triangular cacti with t blocks, t = 0 or 1 mod 4, are graceful, and those with t = 2 or 3 mod 4 are nearly graceful. A necessary-condition theorem cited in the 2020 preprint (graceful implies t = 0 or 1 mod 4; nearly graceful implies t = 2 or 3 mod 4) constrains which type each cactus can carry. I record this residue split as a sharper reading the sources attach, not as something the bullet states.

events.what_happened: Bermond, Brouwer and Germa (1978, Systemes de triplets et differences associees, CNRS colloquium proceedings, pp. 35-38), as reported by Wikipedia's Windmill graph article, show that the Dutch windmill Wd(3,n), n triangles sharing one common vertex, is graceful if and only if n = 0 or 1 mod 4. A search-result summary also says Bermond (earlier work) showed all Dutch windmills are graceful or near graceful; I could not confirm the source for that. Another search summary credits the Dutch case to Bermond, Kotzig and Turgeon (1978) instead; I read only Wikipedia's attribution.
events.delivers: Graceful labelling for Dutch windmills (all blocks triangles sharing one vertex, zero pendant triangles): graceful for n = 0 or 1 mod 4, per the cited source. This is a restricted class of triangular cacti. It settles nothing about the n = 2 or 3 mod 4 residues or any cactus with a pendant triangle.
events.remains: The near-graceful half for Dutch windmills with n = 2 or 3 mod 4 (not confirmed from a source I could read); every triangular cactus that is not a Dutch windmill; the general conjecture.
events.directly_checkable: For a given n, the windmill labelling is an explicit construction from a triple-system or difference construction (not read); a small n can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: Secondary sources only; the 1978 proceedings were not reached. The near-graceful claim for n = 2 or 3 mod 4 rests on an unsourced summary line. Attribution differs between Wikipedia (Bermond, Brouwer, Germa) and a search summary (Bermond, Kotzig, Turgeon).
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for the zero-pendant Dutch windmill class in the residue class the conjecture predicts for graceful labelling.
events.object: Graceful labellings of the Dutch windmills Wd(3,n) for n = 0 or 1 mod 4, constructive (triple-system or difference-set based). The sources do not describe the construction in detail; I did not read the construction.

events.what_happened: D. Moulton (given as J. C. Moulton in one source), Graceful labelings of triangular snakes, Ars Combinatoria 28 (1989), pp. 2-13 (one source gives 3-13). Secondary sources (a 2020 preprint's reference list and summary, MathWorld's triangular-snake page as quoted in search snippets) say it proves Rosa's conjecture for triangular snakes, meaning triangular cacti whose block-cutpoint graph is a path. One source says Moulton used a stronger 'almost graceful' labelling in place of 'nearly graceful'. I did not open the paper.
events.delivers: For the class of triangular snakes (block-cutpoint graph a path): the conjecture's graceful or nearly graceful split, per secondary sources, with graceful for n = 0 or 1 mod 4. Restricted to snakes.
events.remains: Every triangular cactus that is not a snake, including snakes with pendant triangles (the 2020 preprint poses the snake-with-pendants question as open, using Skolem-type sequences).
events.directly_checkable: Individual snake labellings can be checked by hand; the paper not read.
events.doubts: The definitions differ across sources: 'almost graceful' (one source) versus 'nearly graceful' (the conjecture's own term). Whether the 1989 result is the conjecture's exact form for snakes depends on that and is unresolved from the sources read. The author's initial is also given differently.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture for the snake class.
events.object: Labellings of triangular snakes, constructive per the secondary descriptions; the construction was not read.

events.what_happened: Dyer, Payne, Shalaby and Wicks, On the graceful conjecture for triangular cacti, Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 53 (2012), pp. 151-170 (received 3 Aug 2011). Per the journal page: defines graceful and near-graceful labellings, attributes the conjecture to Rosa (1988), verifies it for two families of triangular cacti, using Skolem sequences and a Langford-sequence technique for Skolem and hooked Skolem sequences with prescribed subsequences; notes Gallian calls the conjecture 'hopelessly difficult' (this quote I could not verify in Gallian's survey). The two families are not named in the pages I could read. A search summary says they are Dutch windmills with at most two pendant triangles; unverified.
events.delivers: Verifies the conjecture for two named-in-PDF families of triangular cacti (per the abstract; the families are not named on the page I read). Restricted to those two families.
events.remains: All other triangular cacti; the paper's own text says it extends the discussion for further research and does not claim the general case.

checked_by.who: Australasian Journal of Combinatorics referees and editors
checked_by.what_they_did: accepted and published the paper (received 3 Aug 2011; volume 53, 2012)

events.directly_checkable: Each labelled cactus in the two families can be checked by hand against the Skolem sequence used (the PDF was not readable to me).
events.direction: Supports: verifies the conjecture for two families; no counterexample.
events.object: Explicit gracefulness or near-gracefulness labellings for two families of triangular cacti, built from Skolem sequences and Langford-derived Skolem and hooked Skolem sequences. Constructive. The families themselves were not identified in what I read.

events.what_happened: Alkasasbeh, Dyer and Shalaby, Applying Skolem sequences to gracefully label new families of triangular windmills, arXiv:2006.16396, first posted 29 June 2020. The v1 abstract claims Rosa's conjecture for Dutch windmills of any order with three pendant triangles. The v2 abstract (9 Aug 2021) says any Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles is (near) graceful, which settles Rosa's conjecture for a new family of triangular cacti. The method uses Skolem sequences (graceful) and hooked Skolem sequences (near graceful) across eleven configuration types (a) to (k), with Langford sequences to build the sequences. Published in Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 91(2), pp. 242-265; received 10 Aug 2021; issue labelled Feb 2025 on the journal page; DBLP lists 2025.
events.revisions: v1 29 Jun 2020 (abstract: Dutch windmills of any order with three pendant triangles); v2 9 Aug 2021 (abstract: any Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles is (near) graceful). Journal: AJC 91(2) pp. 242-265, received 10 Aug 2021, issue labelled Feb 2025.
events.delivers: Dutch windmills (all blocks triangles sharing one vertex) with exactly three pendant triangles, of any order, are graceful or nearly graceful, per the authors' abstract. The summarised HTML reading of Theorem 1.1 gives 'at most three pendant triangles', which, with the 2012 two families, would cover up to three pendants. That reading is not verified against the theorem text. Restricted to Dutch windmills with three pendants.
events.remains: Dutch windmills with four or more pendant triangles (the summarised paper gives a partial Theorem 4.2 for four pendants under a placement condition, described as covering only 'many cases'); triangular cacti that are not Dutch windmills with at most three pendants, including all snakes (the authors pose triangular snakes, with and without pendant triangles, as an open question); the general conjecture.

checked_by.who: Australasian Journal of Combinatorics referees and editors
checked_by.what_they_did: accepted and published the paper (received 10 Aug 2021; volume 91(2), issue labelled Feb 2025)

events.time_since_posted: about 6 years 3 months since v1; about 1 year 8 months since the journal issue
events.directly_checkable: A specific Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles and its labelling can be checked by hand from the Skolem or hooked Skolem sequence. The paper gives explicit tables for small orders (per the summarised HTML).
events.doubts: No independent expert engagement with the proof found in the sources reachable to me: the only public engagement is journal acceptance and one later citing preprint by the same group (arXiv:2112.04265). Scope readings differ between 'three' (both abstracts) and 'at most three' (the summarised Theorem 1.1). I could not read the PDF, so the Skolem constructions were not checked.
events.direction: Supports: verifies a further family of Dutch windmills; no counterexample.
events.object: Explicit constructions labelling each Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles by a Skolem sequence (graceful) or hooked Skolem sequence (near graceful), organised into configuration types (a) to (k). Constructive; no non-constructive existence argument is reported.

events.what_happened: Ahmad H. Alkasasbeh, PhD thesis Graceful labellings of new families of windmill and snake graphs, Memorial University of Newfoundland, supervisor Danny Dyer, issued August 2021. The thesis summary restates the three-pendant Dutch windmill result ('we prove any Dutch windmill with three pendant triangles is (near) graceful', settling Rosa's conjecture for a new family of triangular cacti). It also claims (near) graceful labellings for windmills with C3 and C4 vanes, infinite families of 3,5- and 3,6-windmills, and the union of t 5-cycles sharing a vertex (graceful iff t = 0 or 3 mod 4; near graceful for t = 1 or 2 mod 4). A search summary also mentions a sufficiency condition for kC4n snakes (cyclic snakes, not triangular); unverified.
events.delivers: Restates the 2020 three-pendant Dutch windmill result. The other families (C3 and C4 vane windmills, 3,5- and 3,6-windmills, the C5^t union) are not triangular cacti except where every vane is a triangle, and the thesis summary does not say whether its C3-vane windmill results add any pendant triangles beyond the 2020 family.

checked_by.who: Memorial University of Newfoundland doctoral committee (names not identified in the record I read)
checked_by.qualification: academic doctoral committee in mathematics and statistics
checked_by.what_they_did: approved the thesis; degree issued 2021 per the university record

events.doubts: Restates the 2020 result and adds families with unclear relation to triangular cacti. The CMS 2020 abstract says the C3 and C4 vane result covers 'all possible windmills', which the thesis summary does not say, so the scope of that claim is unclear. The full thesis text was not read.
events.direction: Supports the 2020 result (restatement); the additional families are not shown to be triangular cacti.
events.object: The same Dutch windmill labellings as the 2020 preprint, plus cycle-vane windmill labellings via Skolem-type sequences (constructive per the summary).

events.what_happened: Alkasasbeh, Dyer and Howell, Graceful labellings of variable windmills using Skolem sequences, arXiv:2112.04265, first posted 8 Dec 2021 (one version listed). Per the arXiv abstract page as summarised: introduces graceful and near-graceful labellings for several windmill families using Skolem-type sequences, including (near) graceful labellings for windmills with C3 and C4 vanes, infinite families of 3,5- and 3,6-windmills, and a new solution for the union of t 5-cycles sharing a vertex. DBLP (not opened) lists the journal version as Ars Combinatoria 159(1), pp. 109-131, 2024. The abstract does not mention pendant triangles, triangular cacti or Rosa's conjecture.
events.revisions: Single arXiv version listed. Journal: Ars Combinatoria 159(1), pp. 109-131 (2024) per DBLP, from a search snippet; not opened.
events.delivers: (Near) graceful labellings for cycle-vane windmills (C3 and C4 vanes; 3,5- and 3,6-windmills) and the C5^t union. Only the C3-vane windmills are triangular cacti, and those are Dutch windmills already covered by the 1978 result (if no pendant triangles are involved). The C4, C5 and any mixed-vane windmills are not triangular cacti. The scope of 'C3 and C4 vanes' (mixed or separate) is unclear from what I read.
events.remains: All triangular cacti with pendant triangles beyond those already covered, all snakes, the general conjecture.

checked_by.who: Ars Combinatoria (journal of record, per DBLP; not verified by opening the journal page)
checked_by.what_they_did: published the version listed on DBLP (2024, volume 159(1))

events.directly_checkable: Each cycle-vane windmill labelling is explicit and checkable by hand from its Skolem-type sequence; the paper not read.
events.doubts: I did not read the paper. The scope of 'C3 and C4 vanes' is unclear, and whether any mixed-vane windmill is a triangular cactus is not settled from the abstract.
events.direction: Neutral to supporting for the conjecture; its triangular-cactus content is at most the Dutch windmill case, which predates it.
events.object: Explicit Skolem-type labellings of cycle-vane windmills (C3, C4, 3,5 and 3,6 windmills) and of the C5^t union; constructive per the summary.

events.what_happened: Two 2020 talk abstracts restate the group's windmill results. Danny Dyer, Gracefully labelling triangular cacti using Skolem sequences (CMS Winter 2020 meeting, joint with Alkasasbeh and Shalaby): the Skolem approach works for triangular windmills with pendants, and there is hope to label triangular snakes similarly. Jared Howell, Gracefully labelling windmills using Skolem-like sequences (Atlantic graph theory seminar, 25 Nov 2020). Both are dated to the write-up they restate (the June 2020 preprint), so they are not separate results. Their PDFs were not readable to me; the content comes from search snippets and a metadata-only fetch.
events.delivers: Restates the 2020 preprint and the 2021 variable windmill results; the Dyer abstract says there is hope for snakes but claims no snake result.
events.remains: As for the 2020 preprint; snakes remain open per the talk abstract's own wording.
events.direction: Restates the supporting result; claims no new cases.

events.what_happened: Luisa Frickes, Simone Dantas and Atilio G. Luiz, On the Graceful Game, arXiv:2005.05213, submitted 11 May 2020. The paper studies a two-player graceful game introduced by Tuza (2017), with winning strategies for complete graphs, paths, cycles and several families. Its abstract says 'all triangular cacti are graceful (1988)', attributed to Rosa alongside the tree conjecture.
events.delivers: Nothing on the conjecture's status. It is a discounted mention: it misstates the 1988 conjecture as 'all triangular cacti are graceful', dropping the nearly-graceful alternative. It concerns a game on graphs, a different question.
events.doubts: The abstract's statement of the conjecture omits the nearly-graceful alternative. The abstract page shows no reference list, so whether it cites the 2012 or 2020 triangular cactus papers is unknown.
events.direction: Not applicable to the conjecture; it restates a misstated version.

events.what_happened: Christian Barrientos, Two families of graceful cacti, Communications on Number Theory and Combinatorial Theory, vol. 6, article 1 (2025), DOI 10.70013/s8t4q6v1, as fetched from the Kutztown 'Contact' vol. 6 page (the author and venue pairing was not reconciled between the two). Gives graceful labellings for a subfamily of quadrangular cacti (blocks are 4-cycles) whose underlying graph corresponds to rooted binary trees with at most two vertices per level, and proves alpha-labelings for cyclic snakes with blocks C_{4n} and maximum degree four.
events.delivers: Graceful labellings for a subfamily of quadrangular cacti (4-cycle blocks), and alpha-labelings for certain cyclic snakes of 4n-cycles. It is a neighbouring problem: its blocks are not triangles, so it does not move the triangular cactus conjecture.

checked_by.who: Communications on Number Theory and Combinatorial Theory (journal named in the fetched metadata)
checked_by.what_they_did: published the article (2025, vol. 6, article 1), per the fetched metadata

events.direction: Not applicable: a neighbouring problem on quadrangular cacti.
events.object: Explicit graceful labellings for a binary-tree-shaped subfamily of quadrangular cacti; explicit alpha-labelings for cyclic snakes of 4n-cycles. Constructive. Not a triangular cactus.

events.what_happened: Shoham Letzter, Alexey Pokrovskiy and Ella Williams, On the gracesize of trees, arXiv:2511.11331, first submitted 14 Nov 2025. Proves that for every epsilon > 0 there is n0 such that every tree on more than n0 vertices has gracesize at least (1 - epsilon)n, i.e. admits an almost graceful labelling. The abstract restates the graceful tree conjecture, posed by 'Rosa in the 1960s', as the claim that every tree is graceful.
events.delivers: An asymptotic result for the parent problem (the graceful tree conjecture): large trees are almost graceful. It says nothing about triangular cacti; the abstract does not mention cacti.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (the child statement), and the exact parent conjecture.
events.direction: Parent-level only; asymptotic and about trees. No bearing on whether every triangular cactus is graceful or nearly graceful.

events.what_happened: Adithya Kulkarni, Mohna Chakraborty and Jay Bagga, Evaluating Large Language Models on Solved and Unsolved Problems in Graph Theory: Implications for Computing Education, arXiv:2602.05059 (submitted 4 Feb 2026). Evaluates one LLM, not named on the abstract page, on a solved problem about the gracefulness of line graphs (a proof the paper says a graph theory expert confirmed) and an open problem about graceful line graphs with no known solution, on which the model made no progress and acknowledged uncertainty. The page read does not mention triangular cacti, Rosa's conjecture, or any cactus.
events.delivers: Nothing on Rosa's conjecture. It concerns line graphs, a different question. The model's solved-problem proof is for a different problem.
events.doubts: The paper's expert confirmation applies to the line-graph proof only, as far as I could read.
events.direction: Not applicable: a different graceful-labelling question about line graphs.

disputes.summary: Attribution of the Dutch windmill graceful result for n = 0 or 1 mod 4: Wikipedia credits Bermond, Brouwer and Germa (1978, CNRS colloquium); a search summary credits Bermond, Kotzig and Turgeon (1978). Both may be right, but the record gives only the Wikipedia attribution, which I read.

Moulton's 1989 snake result: one source says the paper proves a stronger 'almost graceful' labelling in place of 'nearly graceful'; other secondary sources say it proves the conjecture for triangular snakes as stated. Whether the snake class is settled in the conjecture's exact form is unresolved from the sources read.

The three-pendant Dutch windmill result: both the v1 and v2 abstracts say three pendant triangles (v1: any order). The summarised HTML reading of Theorem 1.1 says at most three pendant triangles, and a separate Theorem 4.2 for four pendants under a placement condition. These readings conflict; the theorem text was not read directly.

Frickes, Dantas and Luiz (2020) state the 1988 conjecture as 'all triangular cacti are graceful', dropping the nearly-graceful alternative that Rosa's statement, Wikipedia and the 2012 paper all include.

summary: Rosa's conjecture (Rosa, 1988, Scientia 1, pp. 87-95, per Wikipedia's Cactus graph article) says every triangular cactus is graceful or nearly graceful. The Wikipedia pages I opened still treat it as open: the Graceful labeling article, last edited 21 July 2026, still calls it a conjecture; the Cactus graph article carries it in an unsolved-problem box; and the frozen list entry, a sub-bullet under the graceful tree conjecture, matches the statement. I found partial results only, and all of them were first written before 26 January 2024: Bermond et al. (1978) for Dutch windmills (no pendant triangles, graceful for n = 0 or 1 mod 4; near-graceful status for n = 2 or 3 mod 4 not confirmed); Moulton (1989) for triangular snakes (definition disputed: 'almost' versus 'near' graceful); Dyer, Payne, Shalaby and Wicks (AJC 53, 2012) for two families (named only in the PDF, which I could not read; a search summary says Dutch windmills with at most two pendants, unverified); and Alkasasbeh, Dyer and Shalaby (arXiv 29 June 2020; AJC 91(2) pp. 242-265, received 10 Aug 2021, issue labelled Feb 2025) for Dutch windmills with three pendant triangles of any order, which the authors say settles the conjecture for 'a new family'. The 2020 paper poses triangular snakes, with and without pendant triangles, as open. The windmill results have a close call on scope: both abstracts say three pendant triangles, while the summarised Theorem 1.1 says at most three; the theorem text was not readable. I dated each event by its first public written version (the arXiv posting or, where none exists, the journal year) as the DEEP_DIVE rules require. The in-window items are: the 2021 variable-windmill preprint (arXiv 8 Dec 2021), whose Ars Combinatoria version (2024, per DBLP) is a journal appearance, not a new result; the 2020 preprint's AJC appearance in 2025 (journal date only); and three discounted papers, the 2025 quadrangular-cactus paper (Barrientos), the Feb 2026 LLM evaluation on line graphs, and the Nov 2025 tree-gracesize paper, which concerns the parent. Two other claims in search results concern the parent (tree) problem only, namely Gnang's preprints and Mehendale's; they are not recorded as events here, and even if accepted they would not settle this child. A 2023 arXiv paper (2307.08039) calls Rosa's conjecture 'one notable example' of an unsolved cactus problem and cites only the 1988 paper, not the 2012 or 2020 work. Semantic Scholar lists two citing papers for the 2020 preprint, one unrelated and one the 2021 windmill preprint. AI search: 13 of the 50 queries combined the problem name or graceful-labelling terms with LLM, GPT, Claude, Gemini, AlphaEvolve, AlphaProof, Lean, Erdos-problem and neural/RL terms, and found no AI system credited with any part of this problem. Tao's AI-contributions wiki for Erdos problems has no entry on graph labelling. The August 2026 AI4Math survey (arXiv 2608.24961) has no keyword hits. The unrelated AI claims I saw in search snippets (a July 2026 cycle double cover claim, a May 2026 unit-distance counterexample, and an unverified GPT-5.6 claim about a flow conjecture) do not concern this problem and I did not open them. The record's 'nothing happened since 2024' reading rests on the first-written-date rule; a reader who dates by publication would count the 2024 and 2025 journal appearances as in-window progress.
competing_reading: The record could be read as showing real progress: the 1978, 1989, 2012 and 2020 results together cover the Dutch windmill class (up to three pendants, per the abstract), a snake class and two further families, so a substantial part of the triangular cacti the conjecture covers may be settled. Against that, every result is a restricted family of a class with unbounded shape, the authors themselves pose snakes as open, and the family-by-family count is the judging pass's call. Separately, a reader who dates events by journal appearance would see 2024 (Ars Combinatoria) and 2025 (AJC) as in-window progress, though the rule in DEEP_DIVE dates them to the first arXiv version.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The full text of Dyer, Payne, Shalaby and Wicks (AJC 53, 2012) naming the two families. (b) The theorem text of arXiv 2006.16396 to confirm 'exactly three' versus 'at most three' pendant triangles and the near-graceful definition and vertex range. (c) The 1978 CNRS and Keszthely proceedings for the Dutch windmill near-graceful status for n = 2 or 3 mod 4. (d) Moulton 1989 (Ars Combinatoria 28) for 'nearly' versus 'almost' graceful. (e) An arXiv advanced search for 'triangular cactus' or 'Rosa' with 2024 to 2026 dates, plus a Google Scholar or MathSciNet citation list for the 2012 and 2020 papers; the two WebFetch-reachable citation lists are incomplete. (f) Gallian's Dynamic Survey (DS6, Oct 2025 edition) graceful-labelling section on triangular cacti, which would show the current survey status and check the 'hopelessly difficult' quote attributed to it in the 2012 paper.
